edges.description: Monoclonal expansion of an adenohypophyseal endocrine cell forms a discrete microadenoma or macroadenoma in the sella turcica.
edges.source: Clonal Expansion of an Adenohypophyseal Cell Lineage

edges.description: A tumor of a secretory lineage continues to make the hormone of its cell of origin, so hormone output follows lineage. This is the functioning arm, and it is why a tumor of only a few millimetres can cause severe systemic disease. The further step — that the secretion escapes normal hypothalamic and feedback restraint — is standard endocrine teaching but is not carried by the citation here, so it is not asserted as an evidenced claim.
edges.source: Clonal Expansion of an Adenohypophyseal Cell Lineage

edges.description: Growth within the bony confines of the sella compresses adjacent structures regardless of secretory status. In non-functioning tumors this is the only route to symptoms, so they present later and larger.
edges.source: Clonal Expansion of an Adenohypophyseal Cell Lineage

edges.description: Autonomous prolactin secretion from lactotroph tumors directly stimulates mammary lactation.
Prolactin excess suppresses hypothalamic-pituitary gonadotropin signaling, causing secondary amenorrhea.
Hormone excess — especially hyperprolactinemia — disrupts normal ovulatory cycling and causes oligomenorrhea or irregular menses in the majority of female patients.
Intrasellar and dural stretching from tumor expansion causes headache, the most frequent presenting symptom.
Suprasellar tumor extension compresses the optic chiasm and causes visual field defects.
Compression of the surrounding normal adenohypophysis impairs residual anterior pituitary hormone secretion, especially in non-functioning macroadenomas.
Mass-effect compromise of normal gonadotrophs can also cause hypogonadotropic amenorrhea.
Anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies (central hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency, and hypogonadism) produce systemic fatigue.

evidence.reference_title: A comparison of cabergoline and bromocriptine in the treatment of hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea. Cabergoline Comparative Study Group.
evidence.snippet: A total of 459 women with hyperprolactinemic amenorrhea were treated with either cabergoline (0.5 to 1.0 mg twice weekly) or bromocriptine (2.5 to 5.0 mg twice daily), administered in a double-blind fashion for 8 weeks and subsequently in an open fashion for 16 weeks, during which adjustments in the dose were made according to the response. Of the 459 women, 279 had microprolactinomas, 3 had macroprolactinomas

nodes.description: Unregulated secretion of the lineage's hormone produces a defined endocrine syndrome: prolactin gives galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea and infertility; growth hormone gives acromegaly or gigantism; ACTH gives Cushing disease; TSH gives central hyperthyroidism. The syndrome, not the tumor size, is usually what brings the patient to attention, and prolactinomas are the commonest.

evidence.reference_title: Pituitary Adenoma Prevalence and Characteristics of Omani Patients: A Single Center Experience.
evidence.snippet: Nearly half (51; 45.5%) of adenomas were prolactinomas while 46 (41.1%) were non-functioning adenomas, and seven (6.3%) were growth hormone-secreting adenomas while six (5.4%) were adrenocorticotropic hormone secreting adenomas.

nodes.description: A pituitary tumor begins as a monoclonal expansion of one adenohypophyseal cell type, and which type it is determines nearly everything downstream. Lineage is specified by transcription factors — PIT1 for the somatotroph, lactotroph and thyrotroph lineages, TPIT for corticotroph, SF-1 for gonadotroph — and the tumor retains the identity of its cell of origin, including its secretory programme. Lineage-specific somatic and germline driver genes differ across subtypes and are indexed on `has_subtypes` and dedicated child entries rather than asserted at this root node. Posterior pituitary tumors arise from pituicytes instead and fall outside this scheme.
